source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. I (Montreuil, 1896), pp. 347–353

30.title: Closing lines (article title not in sample)
30.note: The sample begins mid-sentence at the end of this article.

paras.t: […]denter se habuit, ultra modum, id est valde et ultra solitum communemque ministrorum eventum, non tamen immoderate per culpæ excessum, quia juste sic accidit. Et habuit greges multos, ancillas et servos, camelos et asinos. Quocirca quæri potest, an Jacob usus sit prædicta industria circa oves et capras dumtaxat, an etiam circa ceterorum pecorum greges. Ad quod non videtur ex littera haberi certa et manifesta responsio; sed quoniam infra legitur Jacob eduxisse de Mesopotamia tantam multitudinem non solum ovium et caprarum, sed et vaccarum, asinorum et camelorum, videri potest alicui, quod etiam de illis sic fecerit.
paras.en: […] he fared abundantly, [[30:43|exceedingly|ultra modum]]: that is, greatly and beyond what is usual and the common lot of servants; yet not immoderately, through any excess of fault, for it came about justly. [[30:43|And he had many flocks, maid-servants and men-servants, camels and asses.|Et habuit greges multos, ancillas et servos, camelos et asinos.]] Here it may be asked whether Jacob used the device described above only with the sheep and goats, or with the flocks of the other animals as well. To this no certain and plain answer seems to be had from the letter; but since we read below that Jacob led out of Mesopotamia so great a multitude not only of sheep and goats but also of cows, asses and camels, it may seem to some that he did the same with these too.

30.title_en: Closing lines (article title not in sample)

30.title: De spirituali ejusdem capituli tricesimi intellectu

paras.t: Cernens autem Rachel quod infecunda esset, invidit sorori suæ, et ait marito suo: Da mihi liberos, alioqui moriar. Per Rachelem intelligitur anima contemplativa, quæ contemplationis suæ fructu interno et propriæ salutis profectibus non contenta, invidet suæ sorori fecundæ: id est, per modum invidentis se habet circa animam viri activi, in aliorum conversione et prædicationibus fructuosi, conquerens Sponso cœlesti, et rogans eumdem ut sibi det liberos, id est, per se alios convertat, reformet ac salvet. Cui Christus respondet, ex parte sui non esse defectum. Cui rursus hæc Rachel seu contemplatrix anima dicit, Habeo famulam, etc., id est, carnem istam mortalem cui conjuncta sum, illam fecunda, dando mihi gratiam ac virtutem, ut corpus meum ita afficiam flagellis, vigiliis, abstinentiis, fletibus, atque orationum instantiis, quatenus meritis horum corporalium exercitiorum meorum obtineam aliorum conversionem, eos quoque qui interdum me visitant, tam efficaciter horter et alloquar, ut convertantur atque salventur.
paras.en: [[30:1|And Rachel seeing herself without children, envied her sister, and said to her husband: Give me children, otherwise I shall die.|Cernens autem Rachel quod infecunda esset, invidit sorori suæ, et ait marito suo: Da mihi liberos, alioquin moriar.]] By Rachel is understood the contemplative soul, which, not content with the inward fruit of its contemplation and with progress in its own salvation, envies its fruitful sister: that is, it bears itself enviously toward the soul of the active man, who is fruitful in the conversion of others and in preaching, and it complains to the heavenly Bridegroom and begs Him to give it children, that is, to convert, reform and save others through it. Christ answers that the want is not on His part. Then this Rachel, the contemplative soul, says to Him again, [[30:3|I have here my servant|Habeo, inquit, famulam]], etc.; that is: This mortal flesh to which I am joined, make it fruitful, giving me grace and strength so to afflict my body with scourgings, vigils, fasts, tears and persevering prayer, that by the merits of these bodily exercises I may obtain the conversion of others, and may exhort and address those who sometimes visit me so effectively that they are converted and saved.

paras.t: Deditque illi Balam in conjugium. Bala interpretatur inveterata. Tunc ergo Bala traditur in conjugium Jacob, dum caro ex antiquo fomite vitiisque infecta, rationi subjicitur, et Sponso cœlesti ad serviendum offertur, juxta illud Apostoli, Exhibeatis corpora vestra hostiam sanctam, viventem, Deo placentem (Rom. xii, 1): sicque Christus per carnis hujus obsequium spirituales generat filios.
paras.en: [[30:4|And she gave him Bala in marriage|Deditque illi Balam in conjugium]]. Bala is interpreted 'grown old.' Bala, then, is given in marriage to Jacob when the flesh, infected by the ancient tinder of sin and by vices, is made subject to reason and offered to the heavenly Bridegroom for His service, according to that saying of the Apostle: [[Rom 12:1|present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God|exhibeatis corpora vestra hostiam viventem, sanctam, Deo placentem]]. And thus Christ, through the service of this flesh, begets spiritual children.

paras.t: Sentiens Lia quod parere desiisset, Zelpham ancillam suam marito tradidit: hoc est, anima viri activi, qui præ debilitate opera non valet misericordiæ amplius exercere, aliam quamcumque personam ei subservientem, Christo loco sui assignat, ut per illam fiant hujusmodi, et opera producantur virtutum.
paras.en: [[30:9|Lia perceiving that she had left of bearing, gave Zelpha, her handmaid, to her husband.|Sentiens Lia quod parere desiisset, Zelpham ancillam suam marito tradidit.]] That is: the soul of the active man who, through weakness, is no longer able to perform works of mercy, assigns to Christ in its own place some other person who serves it, so that through that person such things may be done and works of virtue brought forth.

paras.t: Amplius, per hoc quod Rachel desideravit mandragoras Liæ, ei a filio suo Ruben allatas, signatur quod anima contemplativa quandoque appetit bonæ famæ odorem, quam anima habet activa per opera fidei coram aliis facta, quæ designantur per Ruben primogenitum Liæ, qui filius visionis interpretatur, per quem opera fidei (quæ est spiritualis oculus animæ) intelliguntur. Lia autem respondet Racheli: Parumne tibi videtur quod præripueris maritum meum mihi, etc.: quoniam anima viri activi forinsecus occupata, frequenter conqueritur se a cœlestis Sponsi amplexibus impediri, et se potius quam proximi sui animam ad exteriora officia applicari. Cui tamen interdum anima contemplativa condescendens, favet ut ad tempus contemplationis vacet quieti, in Sponsi amplexibus quiescendo: sicque anima activi supernaturaliter fecundata et roborata, rursus generare et pristina virtutum exercitia exsequi incipit. Tandem recordatus Dominus Rachelis, aperit vulvam ejus, ita quod parit Joseph: hoc est, mentem contemplativam tanto implet zelo fraternæ salutis, quod merito affectionis tam sanctæ obtinet alicujus conversionem, per quod arbitratur se ab infecunditatis suæ ereptam opprobrio, nec tamen contentatur omnino, sed alterius quoque adhuc sitit salutem, dicens: Addat mihi Dominus filium alterum.
paras.en: Further, by Rachel's desiring Lia's [[30:14|mandrakes|mandragoras]], brought to her by her son Ruben, it is signified that the contemplative soul sometimes longs for the fragrance of a good name, which the active soul has through works of faith done in the sight of others. These are designated by Ruben, Lia's firstborn, whose name is interpreted 'son of vision,' by whom the works of faith are understood (faith being the spiritual eye of the soul). But Lia answers Rachel: [[30:15|Dost thou think it a small matter, that thou hast taken my husband from me|Parumne tibi videtur quod præripueris maritum mihi]], etc.: because the soul of the active man, busied with outward things, often complains that it is kept from the embraces of the heavenly Bridegroom, and that it, rather than its neighbour's soul, is set to outward duties. Yet the contemplative soul, sometimes condescending to it, allows it for a time to rest in the quiet of contemplation, reposing in the Bridegroom's embraces; and so the soul of the active man, supernaturally made fruitful and strengthened, begins again to bring forth and to take up its former exercises of virtue. At length [[30:22|the Lord also remembering Rachel|Recordatus quoque Dominus Rachelis]] opens her womb, so that she bears Joseph: that is, He fills the contemplative mind with such zeal for the salvation of its brethren that, by the merit of so holy an affection, it obtains someone's conversion, and by this judges itself delivered from the reproach of its barrenness. Yet it is not wholly content, but still thirsts for the salvation of another, saying: [[30:24|The Lord give me also another son.|Addat mihi Dominus filium alterum.]]

paras.t: Præterea, nato Joseph, voluit Jacob ad patriam suam reverti: quia dum Christus multos ex Synagoga tam activos quam contemplativos suo discipulatui conjunxisset, ac regnasset, voluit reverti ad Patrem, patriamque cœlestem. Vir quoque fidelis, contemplativæ vitæ fructu gustato, cupit exterioribus resignare, et interioribus pure insistere; quem Laban cupit adhuc in exterioribus et pristino suo detinere obsequio. Vir autem contemplativus, pensans quantum ex hoc Jacob possit fructificare, eo pacto consentit, ut oves et capræ diversorum colorum, sint suæ, id est, quatenus eos possit convertere, et spirituales suos efficere filios, qui duplicitatis vitio et maculis pravitatum sunt respersi. Cui Dominus in hoc aliquando acquiescit, ita quod orationibus, exhortationibus, meritis et exemplis viri talis, peccatores tales convertit; alios vero greges, scilicet justos, aliis committit pastoribus.
paras.en: Moreover, [[30:25|when Joseph was born|Nato autem Joseph]], Jacob wished to return to his own country: for when Christ had joined many from the Synagogue, both active and contemplative, to His discipleship, and had reigned, He wished to return to the Father and the heavenly fatherland. So too the faithful man, having tasted the fruit of the contemplative life, desires to give up outward things and to apply himself purely to inward ones; but Laban wishes to keep him still in outward things and in his former service. The contemplative man, however, weighing how much fruit Jacob might bear from this, consents on the condition that the sheep and goats of divers colours shall be his: that is, that he may convert those who are spattered with the vice of duplicity and the stains of wickedness, and make them his spiritual children. And the Lord sometimes grants him this, so that by the prayers, exhortations, merits and examples of such a man He converts such sinners; but the other flocks, namely the just, He entrusts to other shepherds.

paras.t: Itaque Jacob ovibus sibi creditis virgas decorticatas et multiformiter coloratas, tempore spiritualis fecundationis proponit, hoc est præcepta justitiæ, auctoritatem ecclesiasticam, potestatem verbi cœlestis, per quæ quasi per virgas corriguntur iniqui et reformantur ac diriguntur, quæ etiam virgæ multiplici sunt decore rectitudinis ac gratiæ decoratæ. Unde et lex Christi virga vocatur, juxta illud Psalmi: Virgam virtutis tuæ emittet Dominus ex Sion (Ps. cix, 2). Itemque: Virga æquitatis, seu virga directionis, virga regni tui (Ps. xliv, 7). Præterea in canalibus aquarum ponuntur hæ virgæ, id est, in libris sacræ Scripturæ (qui aquis sapientiæ salutaris et gratiarum fluentis repleti sunt) continentur descriptæ. Cortex vero a virgis detrahitur, dum superficialis et indiscretus intellectus, aut etiam rigor distortus, a præceptis et documentis atque ecclesiasticis auctoritatibus removetur, ne quis voluntate pro lege utatur, aut præcepta absque dispensatione et vera interpretatione juxta mentem legislatoris jubeat observari. Itaque per hæc oves et capræ, id est, fideles qui ante fuerunt diversitate vitiorum perfusi, fiunt varietate virtutum ornati, per quod homo qui præsidet eis, seu ita eosdem convertit, ultra modum ditatur sobole spirituali ac meritis in præsenti, præmiisque in futuro: quoniam omnium illorum opera bona et salus in ipsum redundant, et ipse cum singulis atque pro singulis coronatur; habetque asinos et camelos, utpote eos qui onus præceptorum cœlestium prompte ac obedientialiter portant. Alterutrum quoque onera sua pie supportant, quatenus omnes simul a Deo portari et misericordiam consequi mereantur, quemadmodum monet Apostolus: Alter alterius onera portate, et sic adimplebitis legem Christi (Gal. vi, 2).
paras.en: And so Jacob sets before the sheep entrusted to him, in the time of spiritual conceiving, rods stripped of bark and coloured in many ways: that is, the precepts of justice, the authority of the Church, the power of the heavenly word, by which, as by rods, the wicked are corrected, reformed and set straight; and these rods are adorned with the manifold beauty of uprightness and grace. Hence the law of Christ is also called a rod (virga), according to the Psalm: [[Ps 109:2|The Lord will send forth the sceptre of thy power out of Sion|Virgam virtutis tuæ emittet Dominus ex Sion]]. And again: a rod of equity, or [[Ps 44:7|the sceptre of thy kingdom is a sceptre of uprightness|virga directionis virga regni tui]]. Further, these rods are placed in the troughs of water: that is, they are found written in the books of Holy Scripture, which are filled with the waters of saving wisdom and the streams of graces. The bark is stripped from the rods when a superficial and undiscerning understanding, or even a distorted rigour, is removed from the precepts, teachings and authorities of the Church, so that no one may use his own will in place of the law, or command precepts to be kept without dispensation and true interpretation according to the mind of the lawgiver. Thus by these means the sheep and goats, that is, the faithful who were before steeped in a diversity of vices, become adorned with a variety of virtues; and so [[30:43|the man was enriched exceedingly|Ditatusque est homo ultra modum]]: he who presides over them, or who so converts them, is enriched with spiritual offspring and merits in the present, and with rewards in the future; for the good works and salvation of all of them redound to him, and he is crowned with each and for each. And he has asses and camels, namely those who bear the burden of the heavenly precepts promptly and obediently. They also lovingly bear one another's burdens, so that all together may deserve to be carried by God and to obtain mercy, as the Apostle admonishes: [[Gal 6:2|Bear ye one another's burdens: and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ.|Alter alterius onera portate, et sic adimplebitis legem Christi.]]

30.title_en: On the spiritual sense of the same thirtieth chapter

31.title: Elucidatio capituli tricesimi primi: Postquam autem audivit verba filiorum Laban
31.note: The sample ends mid-sentence near the end of this article (v. 54).

paras.t: Recitatur in isto capitulo sancti Jacob cum suis reversio ad terram natalem. Postquam autem audivit Jacob verba filiorum Laban, dicentium: Tulit Jacob omnia quæ fuerunt patris nostri, etc., id est, omnes divitias ejus abstulit ei et nobis per practicas suas. Et est hyperbolicus sermo seu per synecdochen dictus, quasi dicant: Tanta abstulit, quod parum nobis remansit. Animadvertit quoque faciem Laban, quod non esset circa se sicut heri et nudiustertius, id est, consideravit quod Laban non habuit se circa ipsum amicabiliter et favorabiliter, sicut præterito tempore consuevit, imo signa indignationis et aversionis ad se, perpendit in vultu Laban; maxime dicente sibi Domino per inspirationem internam, vel revelationem angelicam: Revertere in terram patrum tuorum, etc., id est ad terram Chanaan, in qua Abraham et Isaac habitaverunt, et Isaac tunc adhuc habitabat, eroque tecum per gratiam specialem.
paras.en: This chapter relates holy Jacob's return with his household to his native land. [[31:1|But after that he had heard the words of the sons of Laban, saying: Jacob hath taken away all that was our father's|Postquam autem audivit verba filiorum Laban dicentium: Tulit Jacob omnia quæ fuerunt patris nostri]], etc.; that is, he has carried off all his riches from him and from us by his schemes. This is said by hyperbole or synecdoche, as if they said: He has taken so much that little is left to us. [[31:2|And perceiving also, that Laban's countenance was not towards him as yesterday and the other day|animadvertit quoque faciem Laban, quod non esset erga se sicut heri et nudiustertius]]: that is, he considered that Laban did not bear himself toward him in a friendly and favourable way, as he had been wont in time past; rather, he perceived in Laban's face signs of indignation and aversion toward himself; [[31:3|especially the Lord saying to him|maxime dicente sibi Domino]], by inward inspiration or angelic revelation: [[31:3|Return into the land of thy fathers|Revertere in terram patrum tuorum]], etc., that is, to the land of Chanaan, in which Abraham and Isaac had dwelt, and in which Isaac was then still dwelling; [[31:3|and I will be with thee|eroque tecum]], by a special grace.

paras.t: Misit nuntium, et per istum vocavit Rachel et Liam in agrum ubi pascebat greges. Vocavit quoque tunc aut paulo post alias duas uxores; sed istæ non exprimuntur, tanquam minus principales, quæ et famulæ erant principalium conjugum, scilicet Rachelis ac Liæ, earumque voluntatem sequi habebant. Vocavit autem eas in agrum, ut ibi cum eis tractaret liberius. Dixitque eis: Video faciem patris vestri, quod non sit erga me sicut heri et nudiustertius. Deus autem patris mei fuit mecum; et ipsæ nostis quod totis viribus servierim patri vestro. Littera pro majori parte plana est valde. Sed et pater vester circumvenit me, id est, fraudulenter egit mecum, meque fefellit quantum in se fuit, et mutavit mercedem meam decem vicibus. Hoc fecit Laban infra quinque ultimos annos, quibus Jacob sibi servivit. Oves enim (ut dictum est) in Mesopotamia pariunt bis in anno. Jacob autem servivit ipsi Laban per sex annos, post quatuordecim annos quibus ei pro duabus suis servierat filiabus: et in primo illorum sex annorum, non mutavit mercedem ipsius Jacob, ut dicitur: quia nondum advertit quod fetus primi seu verni temporis, essent ipsius Jacob; et fetus serotini, sui. Sed hoc comperto, mutavit in sequentibus quinque annis mercedem Jacob, bis quolibet anno, ut infra in littera continetur.
paras.en: [[31:4|He sent, and called Rachel and Lia into the field, where he fed the flocks|Misit, et vocavit Rachel et Liam in agrum, ubi pascebat greges]]: he sent a messenger and called them through him. He also called, then or a little afterward, his two other wives; but these are not mentioned, as being less principal, since they were handmaids of the principal wives, Rachel and Lia, and had to follow their wishes. He called them into the field so that he might deal with them there more freely. [[31:5|And said to them: I see your father's countenance is not towards me as yesterday and the other day: but the God of my father hath been with me.|dixitque eis: Video faciem patris vestri quod non sit erga me sicut heri et nudiustertius: Deus autem patris mei fuit mecum.]] [[31:6|And you know that I have served your father to the uttermost of my power.|Et ipsæ nostis quod totis viribus meis servierim patri vestro.]] The letter is for the most part very plain. [[31:7|Yea your father hath also overreached me|Sed et pater vester circumvenit me]]: that is, he dealt fraudulently with me and deceived me as far as lay in him, [[31:7|and hath changed my wages ten times|et mutavit mercedem meam decem vicibus]]. Laban did this within the last five years in which Jacob served him. For (as has been said) sheep in Mesopotamia bear twice a year. Now Jacob served Laban six years, after the fourteen years in which he had served him for his two daughters; and in the first of those six years Laban did not change Jacob's wages, as is said, because he had not yet noticed that the young of the first, or spring, season were Jacob's, and the late-born young his own. But when he discovered this, he changed Jacob's wages in the following five years, twice each year, as is contained further on in the letter.

paras.t: Et tamen non dimisit eum Deus ut noceret mihi, id est, per suam fraudulentiam nocumentum mihi inferret. Si quando, id est dum aliquando, dixit, Variæ, hoc est fetus ovium et caprarum diversicolores, nati ex ovibus et capris unicoloribus, erunt mercedes tuæ, pariebant omnes oves, quæ sub mea erant custodia, varios fetus, id est diversicolores. Quando vero econtrario ait, Alba quæque accipies pro mercede, id est fetus unicolores, omnes greges alba pepererunt. Si hoc accipiatur de omnibus gregibus pecorum specie distinctorum, sequetur quod pactio illa mercenaria, intelligenda sit, non solum de ovibus et capris, sed et de camelis, vaccis et asinis. Tulitque Deus substantiam patris vestri, qua ipse indignus fuit, vel quam ipse habuisset nisi hoc demeruisset: non enim habuit unquam hos fetus, qui devenerunt in partem Jacob, tanquam de jure pertinentes ad se; et dedit mihi.
paras.en: [[31:7|And yet God hath not suffered him to hurt me|et tamen non dimisit eum Deus ut noceret mihi]]: that is, to do me harm by his fraud. [[31:8|If at any time, he said: The speckled shall be thy wages|Si quando dixit: Variæ erunt mercedes tuæ]], that is, the young of the sheep and goats of divers colours, born of sheep and goats of one colour, [[31:8|all the sheep brought forth speckled|pariebant omnes oves varios fœtus]]: all the sheep in my keeping bore young of divers colours. [[31:8|But when he said on the contrary: Thou shalt take all the white one for thy wages|quando vero e contrario, ait: Alba quæque accipies pro mercede]], that is, the young of one colour, [[31:8|all the flocks brought forth white ones|omnes greges alba pepererunt]]. If this is taken of all the flocks of animals distinct in kind, it follows that that hiring agreement must be understood not only of sheep and goats, but also of camels, cows and asses. [[31:9|And God hath taken your father's substance|Tulitque Deus substantiam patris vestri]], of which he was unworthy, or which he would have had had he not forfeited it; for he never had these young that fell to Jacob's share as belonging to him by right; [[31:9|and given it to me|et dedit mihi]].

paras.t: Et modus illius dationis subjungitur: Postquam enim conceptus ovium tempus advenerat, id est, statim quando instabat tempus quo oves concipere debuerunt, ante ipsam arietum oviumque commixtionem, levavi oculos meos interiores, quia subjungitur, et vidi in somnis: unde ad illam oculorum elevationem incitabatur intus ab angelo. Vidi ergo in somnis ascendentes mares super feminas, mares, inquam, varios et maculosos et diversorum colorum. Dixitque angelus Dei ad me in somnis: Jacob. Et ego respondi: Adsum. Ista fuit interior collocutio, juxta quod loquitur Zacharias: Angelus qui loquebatur in me, egrediebatur (Zach. ii, 3). Sic et in Evangelio scriptum est: Angelus Domini apparuit in somnis Joseph, dicens: Accipe puerum, etc. (Matth. ii, 13). In somnis quippe exteriores sensus sunt clausi et quietati, et ita est homo tunc aptior ad revelationes, tanquam minus circa exteriora dispersus, et per consequens minus ab interioribus impeditus; tuncque audit interiori auditu, quid loquatur in se Dominus Deus (Ps. lxxxiv, 9) seu angelus ejus; tunc quoque ratio viget potissimum in Prophetis, et in eis qui desuper illustrantur, quum tamen in aliis dormientibus propter exteriorum sensuum ligationem usus seu judicium rationis sopitum sit.
paras.en: And the manner of that giving is added: [[31:10|For after the time came of the ewes conceiving|Postquam enim conceptus ovium tempus advenerat]], that is, as soon as the time drew near when the ewes were to conceive, before the very mating of the rams and ewes, [[31:10|I lifted up my eyes|levavi oculos meos]], my inward eyes, as is added: [[31:10|and saw in my sleep|et vidi in somnis]]; so that he was stirred inwardly by the angel to that lifting of the eyes. I saw, then, in sleep that [[31:10|the males which leaped upon the females were of divers colours, and spotted, and speckled|ascendentes mares super feminas, varios et maculosos, et diversorum colorum]]. [[31:11|And the angel of God said to me in my sleep: Jacob. And I answered: Here I am.|Dixitque angelus Dei ad me in somnis: Jacob? Et ego respondi: Adsum.]] This was an inward converse, according to what Zacharias says: [[Zach 2:3|the angel that spoke in me went forth|angelus qui loquebatur in me egrediebatur]]. So too it is written in the Gospel: [[Matt 2:13|an angel of the Lord appeared in sleep to Joseph, saying: Arise, and take the child|angelus Domini apparuit in somnis Joseph, dicens: Surge, et accipe puerum]], etc. For in sleep the outward senses are shut and stilled, and so a man is then more apt for revelations, being less scattered among outward things and therefore less hindered from inward ones; and then he hears with the inward hearing [[Ps 84:9|what the Lord God will speak in me|quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus]], or His angel. Then too reason is especially vigorous in the Prophets and in those who are enlightened from above, whereas in others who sleep the use or judgment of reason is lulled, because the outward senses are bound.

paras.t: Qui ait: Leva oculos tuos interiores, vim scilicet imaginativam et intellectivam, quia hæc visio imaginaria fuit et etiam intellectualis, quoniam angelo edocente, intellexit ipse Jacob hanc visionem; et vide universos masculos ascendentes super feminas, adspersos, varios, etc. Quasi dicat: Sicut nunc vides in somnis, sic fiet in re. Verumtamen visio ista recitatur hic incomplete et breviter, et subintelligenda sunt multa. Creditur namque, quod in hac apparitione angelus docuit Jacob totum quod fecit de virgarum decorticatione et positione in aquis canalium, etc., prædixitque ei quid eveniret. Verumtamen in prima ascensione masculorum super femellas, masculi pertinentes ad Jacob erant unicolores, non varii; sed mutata mercede, masculi diversicolores erant ipsius interdum. Ego sum repræsentative, non substantialiter, Deus Bethel, etc.: hoc est, in persona Dei qui tibi juxta Bethel per subjectam creaturam apparuit, etiam nunc loquor et appareo tibi.
paras.en: [[31:12|And he said: Lift up thy eyes|Qui ait: Leva oculos tuos]], your inward eyes, namely the imaginative and intellective power; for this vision was imaginary and also intellectual, since by the angel's teaching Jacob himself understood it; [[31:12|and see that all the males leaping upon the females, are of divers colours, spotted and speckled|et vide universos masculos ascendentes super feminas, varios, maculosos, atque respersos]], etc. As if to say: As you now see in sleep, so it will come to pass in fact. Yet this vision is related here incompletely and briefly, and much is to be understood. For it is believed that in this apparition the angel taught Jacob all that he did with the peeling of the rods and their placing in the water troughs, etc., and foretold to him what would happen. Note, however, that at the first mating the males belonging to Jacob were of one colour, not of divers colours; but once the wages were changed, the particoloured males were at times his. [[31:13|I am the God of Bethel|Ego sum Deus Bethel]], etc.: representatively, not substantially; that is, in the person of God, who appeared to you near Bethel through a created thing subject to Him, I now also speak and appear to you.

paras.t: Responderuntque Rachel et Lia, sine quarum consensu et comitatione Jacob nolebat nec debebat recedere, quia maritus et conjux debent cohabitare, quemadmodum Adam prædixit, Relinquet homo patrem suum et matrem, et adhærebit uxori suæ (Gen. ii, 24): Numquid habemus residui quidquam in facultatibus et hereditate domus patris nostri? quasi dicant: Nihil de cetero exspectare habemus a patre nostro, nec aliquid restat nobis in opibus ejus, quoniam filiis suis deputavit et dabit quidquid adhuc habet; ideo non est nobis causa manendi cum eo quando tu vis abire. Nonne quasi alienas reputavit nos, et vendidit: id est, utique ita nos tradidit tibi in conjuges, quasi fuissemus ei alienæ, ejusque ancillæ, dando nos tibi nudas seu absque notabili dote aut possessione, et vendidit tibi nos pro obsequio quatuordecim annorum; comeditque pretium nostrum, etc.: id est, possessiones seu pecora, quæ ex tuo obsequio acquisivit, fuerunt victualia ejus, quod obsequium fuit pretium, pro quo dedit nos tibi quasi rem venditam.
paras.en: [[31:14|And Rachel and Lia answered|Responderuntque Rachel et Lia]], without whose consent and company Jacob neither wished nor ought to depart, because husband and wife ought to dwell together, as Adam foretold: [[Gen 2:24|a man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife|relinquet homo patrem suum, et matrem, et adhærebit uxori suæ]]. [[31:14|Have we any thing left among the goods and inheritance of our father's house?|Numquid habemus residui quidquam in facultatibus et hæreditate domus patris nostri?]] As if they said: We have nothing more to expect from our father, nor does anything remain for us in his wealth, since he has assigned to his sons, and will give them, whatever he still has; therefore we have no reason to stay with him when you wish to leave. [[31:15|Hath he not counted us as strangers, and sold us|nonne quasi alienas reputavit nos, et vendidit]]: that is, he surely gave us to you as wives as though we had been strangers to him, and his maidservants, giving us to you bare, without any notable dowry or possession, and he sold us to you for fourteen years of service; [[31:15|and eaten up the price of us|comeditque pretium nostrum]], etc.: that is, the possessions or flocks he acquired through your service were his livelihood; and that service was the price for which he gave us to you, as a thing sold.

paras.t: Surrexit itaque Jacob, et impositis liberis, scilicet undecim filiis et una filia, ac conjugibus suis quatuor, super camelos, abiit. In textu autem non exprimitur, an uxores suæ attulerunt secum pueros suos quando vocavit eas in agrum: et verius puto, quod non, et quod post præfatam collocutionem redierunt ad domum, et pueros suos ac alia quædam secum portarunt, propter verba sequentia, præsertim quia paulo post subditur quod Rachel furata est idola patris sui; nisi forte dicatur, quod Jacob in illa vocatione intimavit eis occulte cum nuntio suum propositum. Tulitque omnem substantiam suam, et greges, et quidquid in Mesopotamia acquisierat, etc., scilicet lectos, utensilia, victualia, pecora, pecunias, servos ac famulas. Eo tempore ierat Laban ad tondendas oves: in quarum tonsione fuit occupatio longa, et remote distabat locus ille a Jacob, quum dictum sit præcedenti capitulo, quod Laban posuit spatium trium dierum inter se et generum suum: et ita nactus est Jacob tempus magis opportunum ad fugam.
paras.en: [[31:17|Then Jacob rose up, and having set his children|Surrexit itaque Jacob, et impositis liberis]], namely eleven sons and one daughter, [[31:17|and wives upon camels, went his way|ac conjugibus suis super camelos, abiit]], his four wives. The text does not say whether his wives brought their children with them when he called them into the field; and I think it truer that they did not, but that after the conversation just mentioned they returned home and brought their children and certain other things with them, because of the words that follow, especially since it is added a little later that Rachel stole her father's idols; unless perhaps it be said that in that summons Jacob secretly made his purpose known to them through the messenger. [[31:18|And he took all his substance, and flocks, and whatsoever he had gotten in Mesopotamia|Tulitque omnem substantiam suam, et greges, et quidquid in Mesopotamia acquisierat]], etc.: namely beds, utensils, provisions, cattle, money, menservants and maidservants. [[31:19|At that time Laban was gone to shear his sheep|Eo tempore ierat Laban ad tondendas oves]]: their shearing was long work, and that place was far distant from Jacob, since it was said in the preceding chapter that Laban set a space of three days between himself and his son-in-law; and so Jacob found a more opportune time for flight.

paras.t: Et Rachel furata est idola patris sui, ut occulte coleret ea, ut aliqui opinantur: quod non videtur, quia (ut patuit) assidue invocavit Deum verum pro sua fecundatione; natoque Joseph, Dei beneficium recognovit, et gratias egit Deo. Aliqui putant, quod ex cupiditate abstulit ea, quoniam pretiosa fuerunt, et ipsa patri indignabatur, quod quasi alienam vendiderat eam; et in textu habetur quod furata sit ea, sed non videtur quod fuerit tam injusta. Hinc in Scholastica historia legitur, quod ex Josepho sumptum est, quod tulit ea secum non ad colendum, quia a viro suo didicerat ea non esse colenda; sed ut confugiendo ad ea, veniam impetraret a patre suo, si deprehenderetur ab eo in via. Alii dicunt, quod tulit ea secum, quatenus patrem suum ab idololatria revocaret.
paras.en: [[31:19|And Rachel stole away her father's idols|et Rachel furata est idola patris sui]], so as to worship them secretly, as some think. But this does not seem so, because (as has appeared) she earnestly called upon the true God for her fruitfulness, and when Joseph was born she acknowledged God's benefit and gave thanks to God. Some think she took them out of covetousness, because they were precious, and because she was indignant with her father for having sold her as though she were a stranger; and the text does say that she stole them, but it does not seem that she was so unjust. Hence we read in the Scholastic History, which takes it from Josephus, that she took them with her not to worship them, for she had learned from her husband that they were not to be worshipped, but so that by fleeing to them for refuge she might obtain pardon from her father if he caught her on the way. Others say she took them with her in order to call her father back from idolatry.

paras.t: Circa hoc scribit Lyra, quod ubi nostra translatio habet, Idola, in Hebræo habetur, Theraphim: et dicunt aliqui, quod sunt imagines factæ partim per astronomiam, partim per necromantiam, quæ dant responsa. Hebræi dicunt, quod sit caput alicujus pueri primogeniti interfecti, diabolo immolati, quod præcisum salsatur, aromatibusque conditur, ut valeat diu durare, super cujus linguam ponitur nomen diaboli in aurea lamina, sicque donat responsa. Certum est tamen, quod talia non habent virtutem dandi responsa, nisi in quantum Deus permittit, ut scilicet per ea diabolus ipse respondeat: quod propter incredulitatem et vitia hominum Deus quandoque permittit. Hieronymus quoque fatetur, quod in Hebræo Theraphim habeatur, quod Aquila figuras vel imagines interpretatur; sed Rabbi Paulus affirmat, quod Theraphim in Hebræo non semper significat simulacra facta ad idololatrandum, vel ad responsa dæmonum requirenda. Nam primo Regum quo legitur, Accepit Michol statuam et posuit in lecto (I Reg. xix, 13), scilicet pro David, in Hebræo habetur, Accepit Theraphim; nec est putandum quod in domo David fuerit Theraphim ad usus illos tam vitiosos, sed ad aliquas licitas repræsentationes.
paras.en: On this Lyra writes that where our translation has 'idols,' the Hebrew has teraphim; and some say these are images made partly by astrology, partly by necromancy, which give answers. The Hebrews say it is the head of some firstborn boy, slain and sacrificed to the devil, which is cut off, salted and embalmed with spices so that it may last a long time; the devil's name is placed on its tongue on a plate of gold, and so it gives answers. It is certain, however, that such things have no power to give answers except insofar as God permits, namely that the devil himself should answer through them; and God sometimes permits this because of men's unbelief and vices. Jerome too acknowledges that the Hebrew has teraphim, which Aquila renders 'figures' or 'images'; but Rabbi Paul affirms that teraphim in Hebrew does not always signify images made for idolatry or for seeking answers from demons. For in the first book of Kings, where we read [[1 Kings 19:13|Michol took an image, and laid it on the bed|Tulit autem Michol statuam, et posuit eam super lectum]], that is, in David's place, the Hebrew has 'She took the teraphim'; and it is not to be thought that there were teraphim in David's house for such vicious uses, but for certain lawful representations.

paras.t: Noluitque Jacob confiteri socero suo quod fugeret. Ex hoc apparet, quod Laban habuit Jacob suspectum de fuga, et quod sciscitatus est eum inde, cui Jacob noluit suum confiteri propositum, ne impediretur a Laban. Quumque abiisset tam ipse quam omnia quæ juris sui erant, et amne transmisso, id est fluvio Mesopotamiæ pertransito, pergeret contra montem Galaad, hoc est versus montem istum, qui tamen post hæc vocatus est Galaad, ut in isto habetur capitulo, nuntiatum est Laban die tertio, quod fugeret Jacob. Ex quo elicitur, quod primo die quo Jacob iniit fugam, quidam cœpit ire ad Laban ad annuntiandum hoc ei, quia (ut dictum est) locus ubi filii Laban pecora sua pascebant, distabat itinere trium dierum a Jacob: et forsitan Laban fecit observari an fugeret. Qui assumptis fratribus suis, id est filiis et cognatis, persecutus est eum, etc. Viditque in somnis dicentem sibi Dominum: Cave ne quidquam asperum loquaris contra Jacob, etc. Hoc Deus dixit per angelum, quem Laban in somno visione imaginaria vidit in similitudine quadam humana. Vel sumitur hic, videre, pro audire, sicut in Apocalypsi: Conversus sum ut viderem vocem (Apoc. i, 12).
paras.en: [[31:20|And Jacob would not confess to his father-in-law that he was flying away.|Noluitque Jacob confiteri socero suo quod fugeret.]] From this it appears that Laban suspected Jacob of flight and questioned him about it, and Jacob would not confess his purpose to him lest he be hindered by Laban. [[31:21|And when he was gone, together with all that belonged to him, and having passed the river|Cumque abiisset tam ipse quam omnia quæ juris sui erant, et amne transmisso]], that is, having crossed the river of Mesopotamia, [[31:21|was going on towards mount Galaad|pergeret contra montem Galaad]], that is, toward that mountain, which however was only afterward called Galaad, as is found in this chapter, [[31:22|It was told Laban on the third day, that Jacob fled.|nuntiatum est Laban die tertio quod fugeret Jacob.]] From this it is gathered that on the first day of Jacob's flight someone set out for Laban to tell him of it, because (as has been said) the place where Laban's sons pastured their flocks was three days' journey from Jacob; and perhaps Laban had him watched to see whether he would flee. [[31:23|And he took his brethren with him|Qui, assumptis fratribus suis]], that is, his sons and kinsmen, [[31:23|and pursued after him|persecutus est eum]], etc. [[31:24|And he saw in a dream God, saying to him: Take heed thou speak not any thing harshly against Jacob.|Viditque in somnis dicentem sibi Deum: Cave ne quidquam aspere loquaris contra Jacob.]] God said this through an angel, whom Laban saw in sleep, in an imaginary vision, in a certain human likeness. Or else 'to see' is taken here for 'to hear,' as in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 1:12|I turned to see the voice|conversus sum ut viderem vocem]].

paras.t: Et dixit ad Jacob: Quare ita egisti, ut clam me abigeres, id est me ignorante tam præcipitanter auferres, et tecum assumeres, filias meas quasi captivas gladio? etc., id est violenter: quod falsum erat, quia filiæ Laban sponte ac libenter abierunt cum suo marito. Stulte operatus es, etc., taliter fugiendo. Hoc non est verum, quoniam Deo præcipiente hoc fecit, qui et protectionem suam ei promisit: quod fecit in tantum, quod prohibuit ipsi Laban, non solum lædere aut tangere, sed etiam dure affari pium Jacob. Esto, id est, sit ita, seu concedatur quod dicam; ad tuos ire cupiebas, et desiderio tibi erat domus patris tui, id est, ipsos parentes tuos, eorumque domum et terram optasti videre, quod valde fuerat naturale, præsertim post annos viginti. Cur furatus es deos meos? Laban per propria verba pandit suam stultitiam. Etenim quales dii fuerunt, qui furto poterant tolli? et quomodo poterant custodire suos cultores, qui nequibant custodire se ipsos?
paras.en: [[31:26|And he said to Jacob: Why hast thou done thus, to carry away, without my knowledge, my daughters as captives taken with the sword?|Et dixit ad Jacob: Quare ita egisti, ut clam me abigeres filias meas quasi captivas gladio?]] That is, to carry off my daughters without my knowledge, so hastily, and take them with you as if by violence; which was false, for Laban's daughters went with their husband willingly and gladly. [[31:28|Thou hast done foolishly|stulte operatus es]], etc., by fleeing in this way. This is not true, since he did it at God's command, who also promised him His protection; and He gave it so fully that He forbade Laban not only to harm or touch the pious Jacob, but even to speak harshly to him. [[31:30|Suppose|Esto]], that is, let it be so, or let it be granted, I will say, [[31:30|thou didst desire to go to thy friends, and hadst a longing after thy father's house|ad tuos ire cupiebas, et desiderio erat tibi domus patris tui]]: that is, you longed to see your parents themselves, and their house and land, which was very natural, especially after twenty years. [[31:30|Why hast thou stolen away my gods?|cur furatus es deos meos?]] Laban lays bare his folly by his own words. For what sort of gods were these that could be carried off by theft? And how could they guard their worshippers who could not guard themselves?

paras.t: Respondit Jacob, etc.: Scrutare, etc. Hæc dicens, ignorabat quod Rachel furata esset idola. Quumque intrasset tentorium Rachelis: quælibet enim uxorum Jacob habuit proprium tabernaculum, in quo cum sua sobole erat et operabatur; illa festinans, abscondit idola subter stramenta cameli, et sedit desuper. Hoc verbum, abscondit, est hic præteriti temporis. Nam interim quod Laban scrutabatur tentoria Jacob et aliarum uxorum ipsius, Rachel festinanter occultavit idola sub stramentis, per quæ quidam intelligunt sellam cameli; sed incertum videtur quod sub sella poterant tegi, quamvis et ipsa desuper sedit: ideo per stramenta cameli, possunt intelligi fimus et alia quæ sub camelo ponuntur. Scrutantique omne tentorium et nihil invenienti, ait Rachel: Ne irascatur dominus meus quod coram te assurgere nequeo, quia juxta consuetudinem feminarum nunc accidit mihi, id est, improvisa atque feminea debilitas seu fluxus menstrualis non permittit me surgere. Unde secundum Josephum, dixit naturalem purgationem sibimet imminere, et hoc fuit mendacium ad minus officiosum. Sic delusa sollicitudo quærentis est: quia per tam curialem et apparentem locutionem fuit deceptus.
paras.en: [[31:31|Jacob answered|Respondit Jacob]], etc.: [[31:32|Search|scrutare]], etc. [[31:32|Now when he said this, he knew not that Rachel had stolen the idols.|Hæc dicens, ignorabat quod Rachel furata esset idola.]] [[31:33|And when he was entered into Rachel's tent|Cumque intrasset tentorium Rachelis]] (for each of Jacob's wives had her own tent, in which she lived and worked with her children), [[31:34|She, in haste, hid the idols under the camel's furniture, and sat upon them|illa festinans abscondit idola subter stramenta cameli, et sedit desuper]]. The word 'hid' here has the force of a past tense: for while Laban was searching the tents of Jacob and of his other wives, Rachel hastily concealed the idols under the furniture, by which some understand the camel's saddle; but it seems doubtful that they could be hidden under the saddle, even though she sat on top of it; so by the camel's furniture may be understood the straw and other things laid under a camel. [[31:34|And when he had searched all the tent, and found nothing|scrutantique omne tentorium, et nihil invenienti]], Rachel said: [[31:35|Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise up before thee, because it has now happened to me according to the custom of women.|Ne irascatur dominus meus quod coram te assurgere nequeo: quia juxta consuetudinem feminarum nunc accidit mihi.]] That is, an unforeseen womanly weakness, the monthly flow, does not permit me to rise. Hence, according to Josephus, she said that her natural purgation was upon her; and this was at the least an officious lie [that is, a lie told to avert harm, not a malicious one]. [[31:35|So his careful search was in vain|sic delusa sollicitudo quærentis est]], because he was deceived by so courteous and plausible a speech.

paras.t: Tumensque Jacob, cum jurgio, id est juste indignans, aut etiam motum aliquem venialiter culpabilem animositatis et iræ atque impatientiæ habens, quoniam contumeliosum fuit ita de furto impeti, reprehendi et examinari, ait: Quam ob culpam meam, etc., sic scrutatus es, etc.? quid invenisti de cuncta substantia domus tuæ? id est, si aliquid de tua substantia invenisti in tabernaculis meis: pone coram fratribus meis et fratribus tuis, etc., hoc est coram filiis et cognatis nostris hic congregatis. Idcirco per viginti annos fui tecum? etc. Quasi dicat: Ingratus es beneficiis meis. Ego damnum omne reddebam, etc., id est, pecora furto ablata, et a bestiis devorata exigebas a me, et satisfeci tibi, ac solvi hujusmodi damna. Die noctuque æstu urebar et gelu, etc., id est, nunc ardore solis, nunc frigore noctis ac hiemis affligebar, circa pecora occupatus. Nisi Deus patris, id est avi mei Abraham, et timor Isaac, hoc est Deus quem super omnia timet Isaac, de quo loquitur Isaias, Dominum exercituum sanctificate, ipse timor vester, et ipse tremor vester (Is. viii, 13): unde ad insinuandum quam summe metuendus sit Deus, et quam specialiter timuit eum Isaac, dictum est quasi in abstracto, Nisi timor Isaac; affuisset mihi, forsitan modo nudum me dimisisses, hoc est utique satis probabile.
paras.en: [[31:36|And Jacob being angry, said in a chiding manner|Tumensque Jacob, cum jurgio ait]]: that is, being justly indignant, or even having some movement of animosity, anger and impatience that was venially blameworthy, since it was insulting to be thus assailed with a charge of theft, rebuked and examined: [[31:36|For what fault of mine|Quam ob culpam meam]], etc., hast thou so [[31:37|searched all my household stuff? What hast thou found of all the substance of thy house?|scrutatus es omnem supellectilem meam? quid invenisti de cuncta substantia domus tuæ?]] That is, if you have found any of your substance in my tents, [[31:37|lay it here before my brethren, and thy brethren|pone hic coram fratribus meis, et fratribus tuis]], etc., that is, before our sons and kinsmen gathered here. [[31:38|Have I, therefore, been with thee twenty years?|Idcirco viginti annis fui tecum?]] etc. As if to say: You are ungrateful for my benefits. [[31:39|I made good all the damage|ego damnum omne reddebam]], etc.: that is, you demanded of me the cattle carried off by theft and devoured by beasts, and I made satisfaction to you and paid for such losses. [[31:40|Day and night was I parched with heat, and with frost|die noctuque æstu urebar, et gelu]], etc.: that is, I was afflicted now by the burning of the sun, now by the cold of night and of winter, while busy about the flocks. [[31:42|Unless the God of my father, Abraham|Nisi Deus patris mei Abraham]] ('my father,' that is, my grandfather), [[31:42|and the fear of Isaac|et timor Isaac]], that is, the God whom Isaac fears above all things, of whom Isaias speaks: [[Is 8:13|Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself: and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.|Dominum exercituum ipsum sanctificate; ipse pavor vester, et ipse terror vester.]] Hence, to suggest how supremely God is to be feared, and how especially Isaac feared Him, it is said as if in the abstract, 'unless the fear of Isaac'; [[31:42|had stood by me, peradventure now thou hadst sent me away naked|affuisset mihi, forsitan modo nudum me dimisisses]]: that is, this is certainly quite probable.

paras.t: Circa hoc quærit Rabbi Paulus, cur Jacob distincte ait de Deo et de Abraham ac Isaac, Nisi Deus Abraham et timor Isaac. Ad quod (ut refert quidam) Hebræi respondent, quod Deus non vocatur Deus alicujus singularis personæ, quamdiu vivit in sæculo isto, quia potest mutari de bono in malum; et Abraham jam obierat, et Isaac adhuc vixerat, quando Jacob hæc protulit, ideo ita locutus est. Sed responsio ista non valet, quum supra legatur Eliezer Abrahæ procurator, quum ivisset pro Rebecca, dixisse: Domine, Deus domini mei Abraham, occurre hodie mihi (Gen. xxiv, 12). Deus quoque dixit Abrahæ adhuc viventi, ut sim Deus tuus, et Deus seminis tui (Gen. xvii, 7). Elias quoque in sæculo isto frequenter locutus est, Domine, Deus meus (III Reg. xvii, 20, 21); imo capitulo immediate sequente ait Jacob, Deus patris mei Isaac (Gen. xxxii, 9).
paras.en: On this Rabbi Paul asks why Jacob speaks of God distinctly with Abraham and with Isaac: [[31:42|the God of my father, Abraham, and the fear of Isaac|Deus patris mei Abraham, et timor Isaac]]. To which (as someone reports) the Hebrews answer that God is not called the God of any individual person as long as he lives in this world, because he can be changed from good to evil; and Abraham was already dead, while Isaac was still living, when Jacob spoke these words; therefore he spoke thus. But this answer does not hold, since we read above that Eliezer, Abraham's steward, when he had gone for Rebecca, said: [[Gen 24:12|O Lord, the God of my master, Abraham, meet me today, I beseech thee|Domine Deus domini mei Abraham, occurre, obsecro, mihi hodie]]. God also said to Abraham while he was still living, [[Gen 17:7|to be a God to thee, and to thy seed|ut sim Deus tuus, et seminis tui]]. Elias too, in this world, often said, [[3 Kings 17:20|O Lord, my God|Domine Deus meus]]; indeed, in the very next chapter Jacob says, [[Gen 32:9|God of my father Isaac|Deus patris mei Isaac]].

paras.t: Respondit Laban: Filiæ meæ, scilicet tuæ uxores, et filii, et greges tui, et omnia quæ cernis hic pertinere ad te, mea sunt. Si voluit dicere Laban, quod erant sui juris atque dominii, falsum erat; si autem, quod erant sibi propinqui, seu a se et a pecoribus suis egressa, verum fuit. Quid possum facere filiis et nepotibus meis? Filios Jacob vocat filios suos et nepotes, quasi valde propinquos, tanquam dicat, Non possum rationabiliter eis nocere, quum sit contra jus naturale, et quia a Deo mihi prohibitum est. Veni ergo, et ineamus fœdus, id est pacis et amicitiæ pactum. Tulit itaque Jacob lapidem, et erexit illum in titulum, hoc est, in signum et testimonium confœderationis atque concordiæ, statuit lapidem illum. Dixitque fratribus suis, id est filiis et consanguineis: Afferte lapides. Qui congregantes lapides, fecerunt tumulum magnum, comederuntque super eum, in protestationem quod essent confœderati. Vidit enim Laban Deum esse pro Jacob; propter quod non audebat ei resistere, et etiam emollitus fuit ex commemoratione beneficiorum et obsequiorum, quæ Jacob retulit se illi exhibuisse. Quem vocavit Laban Tumulum testis, id est tumulum qui est testis initæ pacis, et Jacob Acervum testimonii, uterque juxta proprietatem linguæ suæ. Jacob enim imposuit nomen Hebræum, Laban Syrum: et ambo nomina idem significant. Circa quod ait Hieronymus: Acervus, lingua Hebræa GAL dicitur; AAD vero, testimonium. Porro lingua Syra acervus dicitur JEGAR; testimonium, SYNTHA. Jacob ergo acervum illum vocavit Hebraice Galaad, Laban vero Jegarsyntha.
paras.en: [[31:43|Laban answered him: The daughters are mine, and the children, and thy flocks, and all things that thou seest are mine|Respondit ei Laban: Filiæ meæ et filii, et greges tui, et omnia quæ cernis, mea sunt]]: that is, your wives, and the children, and whatever you see here belonging to you. If Laban meant that they were under his right and ownership, it was false; but if he meant that they were his kin, or had come forth from him and from his flocks, it was true. [[31:43|What can I do to my children, and grandchildren?|quid possum facere filiis et nepotibus meis?]] He calls Jacob's children his own children and grandchildren, as being very near of kin, as if to say: I cannot reasonably harm them, since that would be against natural law, and because God has forbidden it to me. [[31:44|Come, therefore, let us enter into a league|Veni ergo, et ineamus fœdus]]: that is, a covenant of peace and friendship. [[31:45|And Jacob took a stone, and set it up for a title|Tulit itaque Jacob lapidem, et erexit illum in titulum]]: that is, he set up that stone as a sign and testimony of alliance and concord. [[31:46|And he said to his brethren|dixitque fratribus suis]], that is, to his sons and kinsmen: [[31:46|Bring hither stones. And they, gathering stones together, made a heap, and they ate upon it|Afferte lapides. Qui congregantes fecerunt tumulum, comederuntque super eum]], in witness that they were allies. For Laban saw that God was on Jacob's side, and so did not dare to resist him; and he was also softened by Jacob's recounting of the benefits and services he had rendered him. [[31:47|And Laban called it, The witness heap|quem vocavit Laban Tumulum testis]], that is, the heap that bears witness to the peace entered upon, [[31:47|and Jacob, The hillock of testimony: each of them according to the propriety of his language|et Jacob, Acervum testimonii, uterque juxta proprietatem linguæ suæ]]. For Jacob gave it a Hebrew name, Laban a Syrian one, and both names mean the same thing. On this Jerome says: 'Heap' in the Hebrew tongue is called GAL, and 'testimony' AAD; but in the Syrian tongue 'heap' is called JEGAR, and 'testimony' SYNTHA. So Jacob called that heap in Hebrew Galaad, and Laban called it Jegarsyntha.

paras.t: Dixitque Laban: Tumulus iste erit testis, id est reale et mutum testimonium, inter me et te hodie, id est pacti quod modo inivimus, imo et de cetero erit signum fœderis hujus; et idcirco appellatum est nomen ejus Galaad, etc., quia Jacob tunc nomen istud imposuit illi acervo. Et adjecit Laban: Intueatur et judicet Dominus inter nos, id est, per effectum suæ justitiæ pandat se inspectorem operum nostrorum, si unquam post hanc horam violaverimus pactum istud, quando recesserimus a nobis, id est unus ab alio, si afflixeris filias meas injuste, et si introduxeris alias uxores super eas, præferendo illas filiabus meis, et eas opprimendo per illas; nullus sermonis nostri testis est absque Deo, qui præsens respicit: hoc est, ego ab obligatione hac ero immunis, nec aliquis hominum poterit me hujus pacti transgressorem ostendere, sed omnium cordium inspector Deus, infallibilis judex ac testis, puniet reum, qui ubique est præsens, et omnia præsentialiter intuetur. Dixitque rursus ad Jacob, repetendo prolata pro confirmatione dictorum: En tumulus hic, et lapis quem erexi in signum rei gestæ inter me et te, testis erit, etc.; ex quo probatur, quod etiam Laban statuit ibi lapidem aliquem grandem, in protestationem et signum verborum et operum ibi mutuo habitorum; si aut ego transiero illum pergens ad te, hoc est, si intentione nocendi tibi pertransiero locum istum versus te, aut tu præterieris illum, malum mihi cogitans, id est, cum proposito nocendi mihi, veneris ultra hunc locum adversus me; Deus Abraham et Deus Nachor fratris Abrahæ, judicet inter nos, castigando iniquum, Deus patris eorum, id est Deus Thare, qui fuit pater Abrahæ et Nachor. Dicitur autem Deus omnium, Deus Nachor et Thare, vel quia coluerunt eum, sicut et Abraham, vel saltem ratione creationis.
paras.en: [[31:48|And Laban said: This heap shall be a witness between me and thee this day|Dixitque Laban: Tumulus iste erit testis inter me et te hodie]], a real and mute testimony, that is, of the covenant we have just made; indeed, it will hereafter also be a sign of this league; [[31:48|and therefore the name thereof was called Galaad|et idcirco appellatum est nomen ejus Galaad]], etc., because Jacob then gave that name to the heap. And Laban added: [[31:49|The Lord behold and judge between us|Intueatur et judicet Dominus inter nos]], that is, may He show Himself the beholder of our deeds by the effect of His justice, if ever after this hour we violate this covenant, [[31:49|when we shall be gone one from the other|quando recesserimus a nobis]]: [[31:50|If thou afflict my daughters, and if thou bring in other wives over them|si afflixeris filias meas, et si introduxeris alias uxores super eas]] unjustly, preferring them to my daughters and oppressing these through them, [[31:50|none is witness of our speech but God, who is present and beholdeth|nullus sermonis nostri testis est absque Deo, qui præsens respicit]]: that is, I shall be free of this obligation, nor will any man be able to show me a transgressor of this pact; but God, the searcher of all hearts, the infallible judge and witness, who is everywhere present and beholds all things as present, will punish the guilty one. [[31:51|And he said again to Jacob|Dixitque rursus ad Jacob]], repeating what had been said, in confirmation: [[31:51|Behold this heap, and the stone which I have set up between me and thee|En tumulus hic, et lapis quem erexi inter me et te]] as a sign of what was done [[31:52|Shall be a witness|testis erit]], etc. From this it is proved that Laban too set up some great stone there, in witness and sign of the words and deeds that passed between them there. [[31:52|If either I shall pass beyond it going towards thee|si aut ego transiero illum pergens ad te]], that is, if I pass beyond this place toward you with intent to harm you, [[31:52|or thou shalt pass beyond it thinking harm to me|aut tu præterieris, malum mihi cogitans]], that is, if you come beyond this place against me with the purpose of harming me, [[31:53|The God of Abraham, and the God of Nachor|Deus Abraham, et Deus Nachor]], Abraham's brother, [[31:53|judge between us|judicet inter nos]], by punishing the wicked one, [[31:53|the God of their father|Deus patris eorum]], that is, the God of Thare, who was the father of Abraham and Nachor. God is called the God of all, and the God of Nachor and Thare, either because they worshipped Him as Abraham did, or at least by reason of creation.

paras.t: Juravit ergo Jacob se servaturum hoc pactum, per timorem patris sui Isaac, juxta sensum expositum, vel ut aliqui dicunt, et Rabbi Paulus tangit, per timorem quem habuit Isaac, quando putavit se offerendum Deo in holocaustum. Consueverunt etenim homines per terribilia quædam jurare, sicut per horam mortis suæ, aut per diem sui judicii. Immolatisque victimis in monte Galaad, quas obtulit Jacob Deo pro gratiarum actione, quod ita protexit se, et de mutua pace providit, poteratque Jacob tanquam sacerdos offerre privilegio et jure primogenituræ ad se devolutæ, vocavit fratres suos, id est filios et propinquos, ut comederent panem, id est cibos ibi paratos, cum gaudio epulan[di] …
paras.en: [[31:53|And Jacob swore by the fear of his father Isaac|Juravit ergo Jacob per timorem patris sui Isaac]] that he would keep this covenant, according to the sense explained above; or, as some say and Rabbi Paul touches upon, by the fear Isaac had when he thought he was to be offered to God as a holocaust. For men were accustomed to swear by certain terrible things, such as the hour of their death or the day of their judgment. [[31:54|And after he had offered sacrifices in the mountain|immolatisque victimis in monte]], which Jacob offered to God in thanksgiving because He had so protected him and provided for their mutual peace (and Jacob could offer as a priest, by the privilege and right of the firstborn which had passed to him), [[31:54|he called his brethren to eat bread|vocavit fratres suos ut ederent panem]], that is, his sons and kinsmen, to eat the food prepared there, feasting with joy […]

31.title_en: Explanation of the thirty-first chapter: “But after that he had heard the words of the sons of Laban”
